name: Beth Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the wrapping and cartoning end of a packaging line at a food factory that makes cereal bars. The bars come off the cooling belt, my flow-wrapper seals each one in foil, then the cartoner folds the boxes and drops twelve bars in. My day is mostly chasing jams, changing film reels and adjusting temperatures so the seals don't split. When it's running sweet it's like watching a dance, and when it's not I'm on my knees with a torch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else fills your day, at work or outside it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a bit of a nerd for the control panel. I ask an AI chat app questions every day, like why a sensor keeps tripping, and lately I've been using it to teach myself how PLCs work, those are the little computers that run the line. I live with my partner Marco, he's a hospital porter, in a rented place near the station. And I'm on the workers' health and safety committee, which I took because nobody else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that's a bit of a letdown. I'd post something like “turns out the robots were just autocomplete with a marketing budget”. At work I'd tell the lads they can stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep the job I've got and keep tinkering. I'd still use AI to learn stuff, it's just useful, plateau or not. I'd probably be a bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching myself the PLC stuff and ask the engineering manager if I can shadow the maintenance team one day a week. I'd keep putting about a hundred and twenty a month into savings, so we stay at roughly four months. Maybe push the union to get a training budget in the next agreement, since nobody's using the excuse of robots anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little flat. Like a film that ends without the twist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit bored. What would you want from work if nothing big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to understand the whole line, not just my end. Right now if the mixer upstream goes down I just stand there. I'd like to be the person they call, not the person who waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think everyone on your line would feel the same relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's fair. Jean on the packing table would be relieved, she's been dreading it for years. For her, boring is safe, and I get that even if it's not me.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown and post something like “the robots were just autocomplete with a marketing budget”. At work I'd tell the lads they can stop worrying.
S0.think: It means I keep my job and keep tinkering with AI to learn, because it's useful either way. If I'm honest I'd be a bit bored.
S0.do: Keeps teaching herself PLC programming and asks to shadow the maintenance team one day a week. Saves about 120 a month and pushes the union for a training budget.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a film without a twist.
S0.quote: I'd like to be the person they call, not the person who waits.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is one of the few people I've met who finds the calm picture disappointing. She's already using AI daily to learn about the machines she runs. Her ambition is to understand the whole line rather than just her end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the union to grab training and new roles for the people on the floor before management hires them in from outside. I'd post a thread about what a fair deal looks like. I'd probably annoy people with how much I talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. My job's the kind a robot can take, sure, but the job of keeping the robots running is the kind I want. The worry's more for people around me than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening course in industrial automation at the technical college, it's two nights a week for a year and about nine hundred. I'd pay it myself if I had to, but I'd ask the company first. And I'd volunteer to be on any committee that decides how new machines come in, so the floor gets a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited. Then guilty for being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Jean on the packing table is fifty-eight and has done that job since before I was born. If I'm excited, it's partly because I'm young and I like gadgets. That's luck, not virtue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair deal look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training on paid time, not our evenings. First pick of any new tech jobs for the people already here, before they advertise outside. And if the line runs with fewer people, the hours saved get shared out, not just the jobs cut.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the union should grab training and new roles for floor workers before management hires from outside. I'd post a thread about what a fair deal looks like.
S1.think: My job can be taken by a robot, but keeping the robots running is exactly what I want to do. I'd likely do well, and I worry more for the people around me.
S1.do: Enrols in a year-long evening course in industrial automation, about 900, asking the company to pay first. Volunteers for any committee on how new machines are introduced.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, followed by guilt about being excited.
S1.quote: If I'm excited, it's partly because I'm young and I like gadgets. That's luck, not virtue.
S1.fieldNote: Beth expects to come out ahead and is self-aware that this is luck of age and temperament. She immediately thinks of an older colleague, Jean. Her plan mixes self-funded study with pushing for workers' voice on new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop pretending the market will sort it out. Emergency wage support, a pause on mass layoffs, and the companies who own the machines paying for it. I'd be posting every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Even me, with my PLC hobby, I don't think that saves me in two years. If AI can do any job and there are robots to do the hands-on stuff, then fixing the robots is just another job it can do. I'd have a head start of a few months, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still finish the automation course, because I'd rather be the last one out than the first. I'd move savings into an account we don't touch and try to get to six months, so about three hundred a month and no new phone. And I'd get properly involved with the union and with whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income, phone banking, marches, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my stomach would be tight all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the head start buys you only a few months. Is that worth the effort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not financially. But a few months of wages is a few months more to work out the next thing, and I'd learn how the machines think, which helps me argue about them. I'd rather know than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marco do about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go through the bank app on a Sunday and cut everything that isn't rent, food and bills. Marco's job in the hospital might last a bit longer, but robots can push trolleys too. We'd probably talk to my mum about moving back into her spare room if it got bad, which neither of us wants.

S2.say: I'd say stop pretending the market will sort it out, and call for emergency wage support, a pause on mass layoffs and the machine owners paying for it. I'd post every day.
S2.think: Even with my PLC hobby, two years isn't enough, because fixing robots is just another job AGI could do. I'd get a few months' head start at most.
S2.do: Finishes the automation course anyway and builds savings toward six months at about 300 a month. Joins union and basic income campaigns, including phone banking and marches.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight stomach all the time, though not frozen.
S2.quote: If AI can do any job and there are robots to do the hands-on stuff, then fixing the robots is just another job it can do.
S2.fieldNote: Beth's usual optimism runs into the logic of the card, and she follows that logic honestly rather than reassuring herself. She keeps learning even though it may only buy months. Her politics turn more active in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this fairly if we start this year. Workers on the boards of companies bringing robots in, retraining paid for by them, and a plan for what people do after. I'd be saying it everywhere, union, online, the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, the end point's the same, but five years means I could get two or three good years as an automation tech. That's real money and real experience. After that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the course in year one, then apply for maintenance or controls jobs, here or at the drinks plant across town that's already putting in robot palletisers. I'd keep saving around two hundred a month. I'd help run a union study group so other operators could learn the basics with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's energy in it. I'd have a plan and something to do on Tuesday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave your current factory for one with more robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the pay and the training were better. I like my line, but I'm not sentimental about it. The people I'd miss, the machines not so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the study group you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's just an idea, but say six of us meet in the canteen after the late shift on Tuesdays, and I show what I've learned about PLCs and robot cells. Free, no exams. If I'm going to get a head start, I'd rather drag a few people with me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this fairly if we start now: workers on company boards, robot owners paying for retraining, and a plan for afterwards. I'd say it everywhere.
S3.think: Five years means two or three good years as an automation tech, which is real money and experience. After that, I honestly don't know.
S3.do: Finishes the automation course in year one and applies for maintenance or controls roles, including at a drinks plant installing robot palletisers. Saves about 200 a month and helps run a union study group.
S3.feel: Uneasy but energised, with a plan and something to do on Tuesday nights.
S3.quote: I like my line, but I'm not sentimental about it. The people I'd miss, the machines not so much.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Beth is willing to change employer to follow the robots. She sees the window as a few good years rather than safety. Her habit of bringing others along shows again in the study group idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disgrace if we waste it. Shorter working weeks, a public fund from the profits, and free college for anyone who wants to switch. I'd probably run for something on the union executive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have a proper career out of this. I'd be thirty-seven at the end, with ten years in automation behind me. Even if robots eventually do that too, I'd be one of the people who helped set it up, and I'd hope that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, finish the course. Years two to four, move into controls engineering, maybe do the two-year technical diploma part time. And I'd campaign hard for a shorter working week, because if machines do more, people should work less, not lose everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even, though I know that's partly my personality.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning a shorter week. Why that, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my granddad worked six days a week at the steelworks and died at sixty-four. If robots can make the cereal bars, I'd like Marco and me to have Fridays together. That seems like the point of any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marco plan for, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a kid, in a few years, once I'm settled in a better-paid job. And maybe a small place of our own. With ten years I'd feel I could plan things like that without it being reckless.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it and a disgrace if we waste it, and call for shorter weeks, a public fund from profits and free college. I might run for the union executive.
S4.think: I'd have a proper career out of this and be thirty-seven with ten years in automation. Even if robots eventually do that too, I'd hope helping set it up counts for something.
S4.do: Finishes the automation course in year one and moves into controls engineering, possibly studying a technical diploma part time. Campaigns for a shorter working week through the union.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, though she admits that's partly her nature.
S4.quote: If robots can make the cereal bars, I'd like Marco and me to have Fridays together.
S4.fieldNote: Beth is calmest of all with ten years and openly says some of that is temperament. Her push for a shorter week comes from a family story about her granddad. She sees the long runway as a career, not just a reprieve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even the stuff I'm learning wouldn't save anyone, and the people on my line would have nowhere to go. What would help is wage support straight away, not after months of forms, and companies paying into it in proportion to how many people their robots replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the good bit. If this goes right, nobody has to stand on concrete wrapping cereal bars for eight hours. I just want the people who did that work to get some of the time back, not just a letter.

headlineQuote: If this goes right, nobody has to stand on concrete wrapping cereal bars for eight hours.
portrait: Beth Diaz, 27, runs the wrapping and cartoning end of a cereal bar packaging line and lives with her partner Marco, a hospital porter. She uses AI every day to teach herself how the line's control computers work and sits on the health and safety committee. She finds the calm picture a little dull, feels excited and then guilty about steady change, and becomes anxious only when AGI arrives in two years. With five or ten years she would study automation and move into controls work, while pushing her union for shared gains and a shorter working week.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because even her own learning wouldn't help and her colleagues would have nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Immediate wage support without months of forms, funded by companies in proportion to how many workers their robots replace.
